Anumati (अनुमति, “consent”) is consent infrastructure for the Digital Personal Data Protection (DPDP) Act. Your existing system sends one request to Anumati. The beneficiary gets a clear notice in their own language, confirms it, and the record lands in a tamper-evident audit trail. Book a call → See our work

India's DPDP Act is fully enforced from 13 May 2027 . The impact sector holds a lot of beneficiary personal data — Anumati helps you get ready. 22 Indian languages Notices in English plus every Eighth Schedule language. The beneficiary picks; you get proof in the language they actually read. Verify three ways SMS OTP, WhatsApp OTP, or a signed image or PDF upload for someone without a phone. Each counts as unambiguous affirmative action. Tamper-evident trail Hashed, timestamped consent artifacts that cannot be edited after the fact. That is the section 6(10) burden of proof, handled. Works with any MIS One API request from your system starts the consent flow. Works with Frappe, a custom app, or a no-code redirect. Live in a day. Many programmes, isolated One account, many programmes, each with its own template, languages, and key. One dashboard over all of them. Withdrawal and re-consent A beneficiary withdraws with one tap and a webhook tells your MIS to stop processing. Re-consent on template change is built in.

chunks.section: What the Act asks of you
chunks.text: The Digital Personal Data Protection (DPDP) Act covers every organisation that handles Indians’ data. Non-profits are included, and size or registration type makes no difference. That makes your organisation a Data Fiduciary , legally responsible for every record you hold: beneficiaries, staff, and donors. ₹250 cr Maximum penalty for a serious security lapse. ₹200 cr Penalty for not reporting a data breach. Now · since Nov 2025 Act and Rules in force The Data Protection Board is up and running, able to investigate and impose fines. Nov 2026 Consent Managers come online Registered consent platforms go live and Consent Manager registration opens. 13 May 2027 Full enforcement Notices, security, breach reporting, people’s rights, and children’s data all need to be in place. That leaves about 18 months . Enough time, starting now.

chunks.section: How we take you through it
chunks.text: Compliance is a change the whole organisation goes through. We run it in five stages, starting with a mindset shift and ending with an audit by an independent agency. 01 Change the mindset From “collect whatever we can” to “only collect what we can justify”. Delete by default, limit access by role, log every use. It is a culture change first and a technical one second, across leadership, programme staff, field teams, and partners. 02 Set up an independent data-protection team A small team of two to five people that reviews every data collection and can overrule programme teams. No sign-off means no collection. 03 Take the two adoption pathways New data follows DPDP rules from day one, which is the easier part. Old data sitting across drives and spreadsheets is deleted unless it is clearly justified, and that is the hard part. What you keep gets analysed then stripped, anonymised, or encrypted. 04 Prepare for adoption Data residency in India, consent manager arrangements, written data policies, and MIS reviews, plus extra care for children’s data and persons with disabilities. 05 Audit and certify An outside independent agency reviews policies, data, and systems, and certifies compliance. You get a certificate you can show your board and your donors. Non-negotiable All data stays in India. Indian beneficiary data belongs on servers in India. Move your tools to an India region with vendor confirmation in writing, or switch to tools that store data here. Children and persons with disabilities The law sets a higher bar: verifiable parental or guardian consent, a confirmed relationship, no tracking or targeted ads, and nothing that could harm their well-being. The data-protection team checks all four before collection. An independent certificate The audit at the end gives yo

A data-protection team Constituted, with the authority to stop a collection. Written policies and notices Including notices your beneficiaries can actually read. India-resident storage Every record, with vendor confirmation in writing. Provable consent Running through Anumati, with a tamper-evident trail.

Guidance from the Act itself Grounded in the DPDP Act 2023 and the Rules 2025, not a generic privacy checklist. The audit is independent The certificate comes from an outside agency, not from us. Much of what we build sits on open-source technology — not a closed stack only we control. Here's why, and what that means in practice. Join our tech team Meet the team

The impact sector runs on tight budgets and long time horizons. Locking an NGO or a government programme into a closed, single-vendor stack makes both worse: harder to afford, harder to leave, harder to inspect. Open, inspectable technology means our clients aren't betting their programme on one company staying in business, staying interested, or staying reasonably priced. It also means the code we write can outlive any single contract.

Much of what we build sits on Frappe , the open-source low-code framework behind ERPNext. It gives us a fast, well-tested foundation for the systems and workflows our clients need — instead of reinventing forms, permissions, and reporting from scratch on every project. A meaningful part of our engineering team works in Frappe day to day, alongside PHP, full-stack JavaScript and mobile development — so it's a real, load-bearing part of how we build, not a marketing line.

We think the impact sector is better served by open, inspectable technology than by vendor lock-in. Where we can, we contribute back to the ecosystems we rely on. That means code and fixes upstream where it makes sense, documentation for the tools we use, and mentoring the developers who extend them. It's an ongoing commitment, not a one-time claim — and we'll keep this page honest as it grows.

The clearest example: the Frappe Mobile Framework , now open source. It did not start as a framework. It started as us solving real, on-ground problems for the social sector — actual challenges, real users — and over time it became the thing we used to build Frappe-based mobile apps faster and more simply. It was launched into the open at Frappe Build 2026 , and it is no longer limited to one team. GitHub frappe-mobile-sdk The SDK itself. chunks.text: By Prapti Bhatia · January 10, 2023 Technology is always seen as an extension or support to our work, but AI-powered chatbots are shifting the game. These systems are often built into messaging apps like WhatsApp. While businesses across the world have deployed chatbots for various reasons such as customer care and complaint registrations, shopping assistants and even for sending reminders of bill payments and receipts, their use case in the social sector is rather low.

chunks.section: Data Privacy- What It Means and How to Safeguard Data in the Social Sector
chunks.text: By Prapti Bhatia · March 1,2023 Technology and the internet play a significant role in our daily lives, and protecting personal information has become a growing concern. In the social sector, the collection and handling of sensitive information from hundreds and thousands of beneficiaries and stakeholders must be done with the utmost care. As a tech company that creates technology for the social sector, we strive to protect the personal information of individuals and communities we work with every day. One of our priorities during the process of developing systems for different organizations is to ensure that those systems are secure. Let’s dig deep into what data privacy actually means and how we can protect the personal information (PII) of our subjects Data Privacy revolves around how we collect, store and share our data and being in the social sector, the data of hundreds and thousands of beneficiaries and stakeholders is collected hence it is important to keep in mind data privacy at all times.

chunks.page: Data Privacy- What It Means and How to Safeguard Data in the Social Sector
chunks.section: Being mindful of what data is being collected? And why?
chunks.text: The moment we decide to collect information on our beneficiaries, stakeholders, volunteers, etc. we have to be vigilant about what kind of data is being collected. Organizations should always clearly communicate to individuals and communities how their personal information is being collected, used, and shared. Provide them with the opportunity to opt out or provide consent for the collection and use of their personal information. You can look at the following list of questions to keep a check that you are making sure the subject is informed and given consent to data collection: Limit data collection to what is necessary. Only collect the personal information that is necessary for the specific purpose for which it is intended. Avoid collecting unnecessary information, which increases the risk of a data breach.In general please try & stay away from KYC data, GPS location, and mobile numbers unless it is required for a specific purpose. Instead of focusing on data collection formats, start from what you want to analyse for decision-making and then only collect data points which are absolutely important. Technical and Organizational measures to protect the data being collected! Organizations that work with vulnerable communities must ensure the security of their beneficiaries’ personal information. By Akshay Saxena · February 21, 2023 Data is the most precious thing in the 21st century and the foundation of most big organizations. Lots of information is freely available on the Internet in the form of data. Organizations can use that free for analysis and making future decisions. But the main problem is it is difficult to copy and paste every time and this will create a problem when you are working on Real-time data. Copy paste method is not relevant. So, What is the Solution? 1.Web Crawling 2.Web Scraping Most of the Information is free on the internet. So, we can use that information for Research, Predict the Future, Insights into the organization and much more depending on your goals. Currently, we are focusing on Python for Web Scraping. Python is a general-purpose language, we can use multiple libraries for scraping. Let’s discuss one by one

Web Scraping is the method to scrap the data from the webpage by using the Id and path. If you want to use the public data which are available on the internet for further analysis, you can use the web scraping technique to extract that data from the website and store it in your local database. Using Python, the Requests library is the most effective library for web scraping. All you need is the URL of the webpage, Pass the URL into the Requests library it will scrap the whole HTML page into your terminal. After that, you can extract the information by using the Id Tag or the Xpath

Just like Web Scraping, Web Crawling is the method to extract valuable information from a web page by automating the URL, But here we are using automation techniques to reach the desired webpage. It means, To create a bot to automate the web page (Most of the time this method is used if the web page requires a login page) and reach the desired or final webpage. Web crawling is used to extract the necessary information and filter out unnecessary information. For example, if Someone wants to get data from Google or any E-Commerce website, crawling helps them to automate the website and reach the desired output webpage to scrape the necessary data. Python plays a major role in Scraping the data. There are multiple libraries we can use for statics and analysis of the data.

By these methods, you can work on real-time data. This will be very helpful for analyzing the data. You can create Indicators to see the progress: Content aggregation: Web scraping can be used to gather content from multiple websites and aggregate it into a single location, such as a news aggregator. Market research: Web scraping can be used to gather data on customer behaviour, such as what products they are interested in, what websites they visit, and what keywords they search for. This information can be used to gain insights into customer preferences and improve marketing strategies.

web scraping and web crawling can be valuable tools for collecting data from the internet and extracting insights from it. They can be used to gather information that is not available through other means, and to automate data collection processes.

It’s important to use web scraping and web crawling responsibly, as they can have legal and ethical implications if not used properly. Organizations should be aware of the potential risks of web scraping and web crawling, such as violating terms of service or collecting personal data without consent. They should also invest in the proper tools and resources to help them collect, clean, and analyze the data effectively. With these considerations in mind, web scraping and web crawling can be powerful tools for gathering insights and making data-driven decisions. ← All insights

chunks.section: Disaster Relief in India: How Can Corporates Contribute?
chunks.text: By Himanshi sharma · January 9, 2023 With extreme weather conditions on the rise in India, natural disasters have become a matter of immediate concern for communities, government, civil society organisations and corporates. Natural disasters cause loss of life, and property, and knock communities back on developmental goals. Typically, disaster management includes five steps: prevention of disaster, mitigation to reduce losses, preparedness for emergencies, response/relief after a disaster and to build lives back. Here, we will focus on response or relief which involves providing shelter, food, clothes, medicines, etc to affected communities in the aftermath of a natural disaster. Based on our work with corporates, here are some ways in which businesses can respond to disasters.

chunks.page: Disaster Relief in India: How Can Corporates Contribute?
chunks.text: The most obvious support corporates can extend is through funding relief work on the ground. The following examples illustrate how funding can be provided: In-kind Donations: Corporates can directly send relief items to affected communities. A few ways in which in-kind donations can be sent are mentioned below: After a rapid needs assessment, corporates should compile a donation kit that is relevant to the communities – for example, milk may not be relevant because of its short shelf life. However, milk powder can be included in the kit. Items with long shelf life or no expiration date, that are also culturally relevant, and of urgent requirement should be put together for in-kind donations. Service Provision: Disasters may sometimes involve the breakdown of critical services, like transportation, telecommunications, etc. There may be a need to supplement government efforts for these services even without a breakdown situation. Corporates that provide these services as their regular trade and business can leverage their strength and can come forward with this offering. For example, a corporate with transportation expertise can offer movement services to nonprofits or the government for the movement of relief items. Amazon's work in Assam Flood Relief in May 2022 is an example of positioning a corporate’s core strength as an offering during disasters. Employee Volunteering: Corporates can engage employees in their disaster response efforts. Along with making donations, employees can support relief efforts in other ways: Suggest active local charities and nonprofits to their corporates for funding, donation support, or employee volunteering SAP’s response to the Kerala floods in 2018 and Tata’s disaster relief framework involving volunteering on the field are some example

chunks.section: What are some partnership models to help channelise disaster response?
chunks.text: Partner with nonprofits: Corporates can activate their nonprofit partner network and look for partners These collaborations are often led by nonprofits, where they are supporting two different corporates for one relief effort and have these corporates collaborate indirectly. Other times, corporates may come together to execute a combined response strategy. Corporates can partner with vendors that may be in their network, or reach out to them through their local nonprofits. chunks.page: Navigating the Intersection of Usability and Accessibility: Crafting Inclusive Digital Experiences
chunks.section: Navigating the Intersection of Usability and Accessibility: Crafting Inclusive Digital Experiences
chunks.text: By Abhinav Tyagi · Febraury 27,2023 Two fundamental concepts stand out in the ever-changing field of digital design and development: usability and accessibility. Despite their frequent interchangeability, they stand for different but related aspects of developing inclusive and meaningful digital experiences. We explore the depths of accessibility and usability in this investigation, recognizing their distinctions, and importance, and identifying ways to combine them for the benefit of all users.

chunks.page: Navigating the Intersection of Usability and Accessibility: Crafting Inclusive Digital Experiences
chunks.text: The foundation of user experience (UX) design is usability, which focuses on how quickly and simply users can engage with a digital good or service. The effectiveness, efficiency, and satisfaction with which users accomplish their objectives within a system are at the heart of usability. It includes features like a simple layout, helpful feedback, straightforward navigation, and efficient interactions. Users can complete activities with the least amount of difficulty when a design is useful, which increases user pleasure and engagement.

chunks.page: Navigating the Intersection of Usability and Accessibility: Crafting Inclusive Digital Experiences
chunks.text: Conversely, accessibility builds on the concepts of usability to guarantee that all users—including those with disabilities—can perceive, operate, and comprehend digital experiences. It includes design factors that account for a range of disabilities, including those related to vision, hearing, movement, or cognition. Regardless of a person’s talents or limits, accessibility removes barriers and gives everyone equal access to information and functions.

chunks.page: Navigating the Intersection of Usability and Accessibility: Crafting Inclusive Digital Experiences
chunks.section: The Interplay Between Usability and Accessibility:
chunks.text: Although accessibility and usability have different functions, they both aim to improve the user experience. These two ideas work well together to create interfaces that are inclusive of a wide range of user demands and preferences while yet being simple to use. For the vast majority of users, a usable design may be simple and effective, yet it may unintentionally leave those with disabilities out. On the other hand, while an accessible design could benefit those with impairments, it might compromise the usability of the design for a larger audience.

chunks.page: Navigating the Intersection of Usability and Accessibility: Crafting Inclusive Digital Experiences
chunks.text: Usability and accessibility are guiding concepts that form the core of the user experience in the digital sphere, not just boxes to be checked off. We take the first steps toward diversity, empathy, and empowerment when we embrace both usability and accessibility in our design activities. In order to guarantee that no user is left behind in the pursuit of flawless interaction and deep connection, let us work to create digital environments that not only delight and engage but also embrace the rich tapestry of human variation. ← All insights

chunks.text: By Priyanshu Pandey · June 16,2023 Exhibit 1: Your NGO/CSR is passionate about a cause. You pitch your people first program, go through the usuals right from pitching, due diligence, documentation, finalizing budget, approvals, and start working on the project to make it a success. Realizing the reach and quantum of the initiative, the requirement for a website, mobile application, and grant management tool springs up, and it is managed somehow. The series of challenges begin because UI/UX was not considered as an important aspect while forming the said resources. The website has all the information, but it was a struggle to figure out the story, program details, mission and vision, and most importantly contact page. No proper navigation menu, cluttered content, poorly done infographics and data, haphazard order of elements, and long loading time were common for both the mobile app and grant management tool. The donors, funders, project implementation team, and field workers find the app and the grant management tool difficult to access. It fails to serve the purpose; instead of making the process lucid, it became time-consuming. And this is where UI/UX comes into the picture. Social impact organizations and non-profits need profound, to-the-point, simplified UI/UX for all their technical products. UI/UX reads for User interface / User experience, and in layman’s terms, it is the interior design for your application or website. It helps your target audience gain a certain experience and reach their desired information through the right placement of content, layout, fonts, style, what goes where, on each page from the navigation bar. Whether you are a CSR/funding agency disbursing and tracking grants on grant management tools like mGrant mForm, it works wonders for you w

chunks.page: Relevance of UI/UX for Non Profits and Social Impact sector in India.
chunks.text: Are all the pages dynamic and mobile-friendly? Is the load speed good or does it need any optimisation?

chunks.page: Relevance of UI/UX for Non Profits and Social Impact sector in India.
chunks.text: Think from the perspective of a new user who has no idea what your organization is, the key initiatives, mission and vision, values, donate and volunteer pages, leadership, etc. On visiting your mobile app or website, will they be able to access this information easily without any hassle? Donation or grant management, due diligence, volunteer coordination, or resource allocation are the most common complex issues for social sector organizations to simplify. UX designers can simplify these processes by breaking them down into smaller, more manageable steps. By employing clear and concise design elements, including well-structured forms, content hierarchy, logical navigation, and visual cues, users can easily understand and complete tasks, resulting in a more positive user experience.

chunks.page: Relevance of UI/UX for Non Profits and Social Impact sector in India.
chunks.text: Accessibility and inclusivity are of paramount importance for social impact and development sector institutions. UX should ensure that the interface accommodates users with diverse abilities, devices, internet connectivity, and locations. This can be achieved through features such as scalable fonts, alternative text for images, keyboard accessibility, and disability support. Additionally, incorporating multilingual support and considering cultural nuances fosters inclusivity and expands mobile applications or websites to reach a broader audience.

chunks.page: Relevance of UI/UX for Non Profits and Social Impact sector in India.
chunks.text: Visual storytelling works as a powerful tool to reach people. Aesthetics are important, but equally essential to prioritize functionality too with UX. By utilizing compelling visuals, such as photographs and videos, the resource can evoke emotions and create empathy among users. Sharing success stories, showcasing the impact of donations or interventions, and highlighting the beneficiaries’ journeys can inspire users and influential stakeholders to engage more deeply with the cause and contribute to the mission. Additionally, using CTA (call to action) for page redirection and following website accessibility guidelines is an unsaid rule.

chunks.page: Relevance of UI/UX for Non Profits and Social Impact sector in India.
chunks.text: Flexibility and adaptability will always be the foremost requirement for an up-to-date UI/UX. Embracing an iterative design process that allows for continuous improvement based on user feedback and evolving needs is essential to stay topical with operations. Regular A/B testing, diverse user persona and interviews, and data analysis can provide valuable insights to refine and optimize the resource’s UX over time, ensuring its long-term effectiveness. Behavior data can help in understanding what design changes work better to improve UX. Even though they have a lot of skills and knowledge, they can’t do everything on their own. This is where a Chief of Staff can be particularly valuable, as they can take on some of the workload and responsibilities, allowing the founders and leaders to focus on the things that only they can do. chunks.section: What I've Learned About Impact, Iteration and Imperfection at Dhwani RIS
chunks.text: By Aashima Takkar · June 5,2025 As Dhwani turns 10, I find myself reflecting on a journey that has been far from linear—but rich with lessons on building for impact, embracing iteration, and making peace with imperfection. After spending several years at the intersection of technology, impact, and data, I was looking to go deeper—not just working on the programmatic side, but to understand how technology could be a tool for systemic problem-solving, that’s when I joined Dhwani two years ago. Since then, I’ve had the opportunity to lead one of our largest and longest-standing partnerships with Amazon, a role that has taught me what it truly means to balance quality, timelines, and empathy, while also mentoring a growing team. These past two years have shown me that while impact takes time, iteration is necessary, and perfection isn’t the goal. Here’s what I’ve learned along the way.

chunks.page: What I've Learned About Impact, Iteration and Imperfection at Dhwani RIS
chunks.text: One of the biggest unlearning moments for me at Dhwani was realizing that technology can solve many programmatic challenges but it doesn’t guarantee that what we expect will fit neatly into ground realities. I saw this firsthand while working on a disaster relief program with Amazon Philanthropy in India. We were entrusted with automating how real-time needs from the ground were captured. In theory, the system worked—it was agile, robust, and connected NGOs, frontline workers, suppliers, warehouses, and program teams. However, we underestimated the sheer complexity of working in disaster-hit zones. A sleek dashboard is unable to address patchy internet, shifting contexts, and emotional and physical toll on field teams . Despite the “right” system, we went through the drawing board multiple times, and simplified interfaces, localized flows, and refined it for each user, from flood-hit villagers reporting needs to warehouse teams handling logistics. We were building more than a product, a process backed by a Minimum Lovable Product. The impact was gradual and visible once the team started trusting the system, data informed Amazon’s strategy for disaster relief in India was in place. It taught me that impact is slow, and that’s okay. Because it’s in that slowness that we learn to design better, respond more meaningfully, and build systems that actually work for the people who need them most.

chunks.page: What I've Learned About Impact, Iteration and Imperfection at Dhwani RIS
chunks.text: We learnt some of the most valuable lessons at Dhwani in moments of crisis.Iteration is not always a structured process, but it’s where the real work happens. While working on the disaster relief platform for Amazon, we presumed everything was figured out—sprint demos were strong, workflows were intuitive. However, during a live load test with real users like NGOs, warehouse teams, suppliers, field partners—the system buckled. Different networks, devices, and operating contexts exposed unpredictable issues. When such setbacks discouraged the team, I stepped in as a leader, not to fix the cracks, but to help my team reassess our approach and question if the product is usable and serving its audience, under real conditions. Iteration is about asking better questions, redefining success, and being honest about what a product can and cannot do. It allows us to clearly call out users what to expect, when to use it, and how it can support them best. Rebuilding with empathy, not ego, has become core to how we work. And that’s what makes the product, and the process stronger.

chunks.page: What I've Learned About Impact, Iteration and Imperfection at Dhwani RIS
chunks.section: Fall Several Times, But Still Get Up – With the Community
chunks.text: One thing I’ve learned time and again is that setbacks are part of the process. It's better to fail in a demo than crash in the field. But even a successful test doesn't guarantee smooth ground execution. And that's okay. It doesn't mean the product failed. It means we're building for complex, human realities. There’s no perfect one-shot solution. Expecting flawless tech, especially when we’re building for human-centric, high-stakes realities, is not just unrealistic, it’s unfair. We design for extreme realities—emergency relief, health access in rural districts, data for farmer collectives, and not comfort.The goal isn’t to be flawless. The goal is to be useful, usable, and honest about our limitations. These moments are not failures, but invitations—to reflect, reframe, and refine. We don’t work in silos. At Dhwani, the program team is just one layer. The real backbone is our product, data, and tech teams—translating complex problems into solutions that hold up on the ground. We bridge the gap, bringing community needs forward and ensuring the solutions stay rooted in them. Over time, I’ve seen us grow in skills and culture. People who've been here longer than I have often say this has been a journey of learning, unlearning, and deep collaboration. Sure, we move fast. And yes, that sometimes brings friction or delays. But there's space here—to ask questions, give feedback, listen with empathy, and most importantly, stay transparent with each other. We’re still building. We’re not perfect—and we don’t pretend to be. Claiming to have it all figured out often means missing what still needs work. What I value most is the humility in how we work. chunks.section: The Real Measure: Problem Identification, Product Uptake, and Impact Strategy
chunks.text: One of the hardest lessons I’ve learned is that low product uptake often comes down to two things: we misidentified the problem, or the solution added complexity instead of removing it. If it doesn't make life easier for users, it won't stick Developing tech for good values is not about instant gratification or flashy launches, it is about real satisfaction when the tool is used regularly, data flows in steadily, and that data feeds back into a programmatic strategy that actually drives impact. If any one of these three—usage, data, or strategy—is missing, it signals a need to rethink. Designing technology for human-centered impact demands constant empathy, simplicity, and alignment with real needs. It’s a cycle, not a sprint. This cycle of identifying the problem, building solutions that truly simplify users’ lives, and watching impact grow over time is what keeps me going. Falling, learning, and rising with the community every step of the way.

chunks.section: Looking Ahead: A Decade of Learning, and Many More to Come
chunks.text: As Dhwani marks its 10-year milestone, it’s a realisation that our journey is far from over. What we’ve built so far, through the trials, triumphs, and countless iterations is a foundation rooted in humility, resilience, and a deep commitment to the communities we serve. As we look ahead, our mission is clear: build tools and systems that truly serve people, especially in the toughest contexts. The challenges will grow, but so will our commitment to innovate with care, collaborate deeply, and center those often left behind. I’ve learned that real impact takes time, iteration is key, and technology is only as strong as the intent behind it. As Dhwani marks a decade, I’m grateful for the journey and energized for what’s next. We’ll keep listening, breaking silos, and building products people not only use but love. With humility and grit, we’ll keep learning, falling, and rising with communities toward a future where technology empowers and uplifts all. Read more about Aashima's work here ← All insights

Amazon India CSR programme management across seventeen projects Problem: Amazon India's CSR portfolio spanned seventeen separate projects and a wide partner network, each reporting differently. There was no single place to see what was running, what it cost, or what it had changed. What we built: mGrant deployed for the full CSR lifecycle, from partner onboarding to closure reporting; Survey digitisation and impact-assessment analytics feeding back into programme design; A shared monitoring and evaluation framework, plus training, for partner NGOs Results: 17 projects delivered together; Pan-India programme footprint; One platform across the portfolio Scale: Pan-India · 17 projects delivered

Landmark Group Mobile health units, governed by data Problem: A preventive-healthcare programme running twelve mobile health units across Tirupur, Kolkata, Ludhiana, Gurugram, Mumbai-Thane and Jaipur needed to show more than attendance counts. Screening data sat with each unit, and nobody could say whether detection rates were better or worse than the districts they worked in. What we built: A governance dashboard following the programme from inputs to outcomes: camps, screenings, NCD detection, referrals and follow-ups; Anaemia, diabetes and hypertension detection benchmarked against NFHS-5 district baselines; Input, output and outcome KPIs with location heat maps Results: 1,48,320 beneficiaries screened in FY 25-26; 2,184 camps held; 12 MHUs across 6 cities Scale: 12 mobile health units · 6 cities · 1.48 lakh+ beneficiaries

What we built: Group-wide monitoring, evaluation and budget reporting in a single system; An approvals and permissions workflow engine matching the group's governance; A mobile field-reporting app used by over 300 partner NGOs Results: 53 group companies on one platform; 300+ partner NGOs reporting; Group-wide budget & M&E view Scale: 53 companies · 300+ partner NGOs
